Supervise
Stephanie, you were my supervisor in my first year. Do you remember?
Of course. You used to arrive an hour before everybody else.
Because you used to check the charts at six. I did not want to be the last one.
I would check every chart myself. I did not use to trust the summary.
Do you miss it? The operating room, I mean.
I miss the team. I do not miss the on-call weekends.
I still do three a month. It is as demanding as it used to be.
It always was. What changed is that I stopped calling that normal.
I used to be a trauma surgeon.
When I was on-call, I would sleep in the hospital.
I did not use to think about data at all.
It was a demanding job, and I loved it.
I have not been in an operating room since then.

I do not miss the hours. That is the first thing people get wrong. I used to work sixty hours a week, and when I was on-call I would sleep in a small room next to the emergency department, with my phone on the pillow. I used to supervise four residents, and I would check every chart myself before I went home. What I miss is not the routine. It is the moment when a patient wakes up and asks what happened. I have not felt that in six years, and honestly, nothing in my new job has replaced it. But I would not go back. The job I loved does not exist anymore. Hospitals changed, and I changed too.

When I started here in the nineties, the hospital worked in a completely different way. There used to be one computer for the whole floor, and we would write everything by hand. If a doctor wanted an old chart, somebody would go down to the basement and look for it, and that could take two hours. Nurses used to know every patient by name, because there were fewer of them and they stayed longer. I am not going to tell you it was better. It was slower, and slower is not always safer. But there used to be a kind of conversation between us that we have not managed to rebuild since everything moved to a screen.
